terms.gloss: The young con man, co-protagonist; the narrator's 'великий комбинатор'
terms.why_hard: Spelling must be fixed once across all three scripts; zh/ja transliterations vary between editions

proposed.ja: オスタップ・ベンデル

terms.gloss: Narrator's recurring epithet for Bender: the great schemer/operator
terms.why_hard: Proverbial in Russian; must be one fixed phrase, not paraphrased differently each time; 'combinator' is a false friend

proposed.ja: 大策士

terms.gloss: Former marshal of the nobility, Bender's partner; addressed by name-and-patronymic throughout
terms.why_hard: Patronymic must be kept (it carries class and formality); Bender's 'дорогой патрон' and 'предводитель' are separate epithets

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇·沃罗比亚尼诺夫
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ・ヴォロビヤニノフ

terms.gloss: Narrator's running name for Bender and Vorobyaninov, from Bender's calling the chair hunt a 'концессия' (NEP foreign-capital concession)
terms.why_hard: Not 'partners': the NEP-era legal term is the joke; needs one fixed rendering with a single note at first occurrence

proposed.ja: 利権屋たち

terms.gloss: Chapter XIII title; the newsreel director's stock command to his subjects, now a Russian catchphrase
terms.why_hard: Must match wherever it recurs in the chapter; the second-person plural directorial imperative is the humour

proposed.ja: 深く息を吸って——あなたは興奮している！

terms.gloss: Chapter XIV title; Bender's fake monarchist underground, parodying Isaiah's 'swords into ploughshares' (перекуём мечи на орала)
terms.why_hard: 'Орало' is a Church Slavonic ploughshare, not 'shouting'; the biblical echo must survive in each language

proposed.en: The Union of the Sword and the Ploughshare
proposed.ja: 剣と鋤の同盟

terms.term: гигант мысли, отец русской демократии и особа, приближенная к императору
terms.gloss: Bender's mock-grand billing of Vorobyaninov to the conspirators; proverbial in Russian
terms.why_hard: Recurs verbatim and in fragments through the book; must be fixed word for word so the reader recognises the refrain

proposed.en: a giant of thought, the father of Russian democracy, and a person close to the Emperor
proposed.zh: 思想巨人、俄国民主之父、皇帝身边的近臣
proposed.ja: 思想の巨人、ロシア民主主義の父にして皇帝の側近

terms.gloss: Supporter of Grand Duke Kirill Vladimirovich, who proclaimed himself Emperor in exile in 1924
terms.why_hard: Reads as a random surname without context; needs a compact gloss so Polesov's 'Так точно' lands as a monarchist oath

proposed.en: a Kirillite (a supporter of Grand Duke Kirill, the émigré pretender)
proposed.zh: 基里尔派（拥护流亡大公基里尔称帝者）
proposed.ja: キリル派（亡命皇帝を称するキリル大公の支持者）

terms.gloss: NEP tax-form category: a self-employed artisan operating a powered machine; used as Polesov's epithet
terms.why_hard: It is a bureaucratic classification, not a description; the joke is the form-language applied to a man

proposed.en: a sole-trader artisan with motor (a NEP tax category)
proposed.zh: 有动力设备的个体手工业者
proposed.ja: 動力付き個人手工業者

terms.gloss: Narrator's epithet for Polesov, the fussy mechanic who owns a workshop and never finishes a job
terms.why_hard: 'Слесарь' is a fitter/mechanic, not only a locksmith; 'интеллигент' is a social type, not 'intelligent'

proposed.ja: インテリ鍵屋

terms.gloss: Stargorod mechanic, monarchist busybody, guide to the fortune-teller's flat
terms.why_hard: Referred to alternately by surname, name-patronymic and epithets; all must resolve to one person

proposed.zh: 维克托·米哈伊洛维奇·波列索夫
proposed.ja: ヴィクトル・ミハイロヴィチ・ポレソフ

terms.gloss: Fortune-teller (гадалка), Vorobyaninov's mistress of 1899, hostess of the conspirators
terms.why_hard: Her name is Polish; keep patronymic, and render 'гадалка' consistently (fortune-teller, not 'witch')

proposed.zh: 叶莲娜·斯坦尼斯拉沃夫娜（女占卜师）
proposed.ja: エレーナ・スタニスラヴォヴナ（占い師）

terms.gloss: Коммунальное хозяйство: the town's municipal-services department, where Treukhov works
terms.why_hard: A Soviet acronym the reader must understand at sight; do not transliterate bare

proposed.ja: 市公共事業局（コムホーズ）

terms.gloss: Soviet office employee; used in 'сопричисленного к лику совработников', parodying 'причислен к лику святых' (canonised)
terms.why_hard: The pun on canonisation must be carried; a flat 'Soviet employee' loses it

proposed.en: Soviet office worker (miraculously canonised among the ranks of)
proposed.zh: 苏维埃机关工作人员（奇迹般被列入其“圣列”）
proposed.ja: ソヴィエト機関職員（奇跡的にその「列聖」を受けた）

terms.gloss: Elected member of the pre-revolutionary city duma (municipal council)
terms.why_hard: 'Гласный' is not 'vocal/public'; the reader must see a tsarist-era rank now politically compromising

proposed.en: councillor of the old City Duma
proposed.ja: 旧市会（市ドゥーマ）議員

terms.gloss: Dyadyev's NEP-era private firm; a mock Soviet portmanteau ('Quick-Pack')
terms.why_hard: Transliteration alone hides the joke; keep the name and gloss its meaning once

proposed.ja: ブィストロウパク（「速包」商会）

terms.gloss: Kislyarsky's cooperative: an Odessa ring-bread guild trading under a Moscow name; the geography is the joke
terms.why_hard: Бублик and баранка are both ring breads; the contradiction Odessa/Moscow must stay visible

proposed.zh: 敖德萨面包圈合作社“莫斯科小圈饼”
proposed.ja: オデッサ・ブブリキ組合「モスクワ・バランキ」

terms.gloss: 'Jupiter' arc floodlights used by 1920s film crews
terms.why_hard: Not the planet or a name; must be a film lighting term in each language

proposed.ja: ジュピター・ライト（撮影用アーク灯）

terms.gloss: Bender's mock-fashionable label for anything pretentiously up to date
terms.why_hard: Attributed to Bender as his catchword; render identically every time

proposed.ja: 「シック・モダン」

terms.term: акробаты фарса, гиены пера, виртуозы ротационных машин
terms.gloss: Treukhov's drunken philippic against the bourgeois press; the phrases became proverbial
terms.why_hard: Parody of Soviet newspaper invective; keep the triple structure and mock-grandeur

proposed.en: these acrobats of farce, these hyenas of the pen, these virtuosos of the rotary press
proposed.zh: 这些闹剧的杂技演员，这些笔杆子的鬣狗，这些轮转印刷机的大师
proposed.ja: 茶番の軽業師ども、ペンのハイエナども、輪転機の名手ども

terms.gloss: Polesov's mangled bureaucratese ('given the presence of absence'); a proverbial phrase
terms.why_hard: Must sound like a stalled official formula, not be smoothed into sense

proposed.en: In view of the presence of absence…
proposed.ja: 不在の存在に鑑みまして……

terms.gloss: Formula of tsarist decrees ('has been graciously pleased to command'), the only imperial phrase Bender can recall
terms.why_hard: Needs a recognisably archaic court register in each target

proposed.en: has been graciously pleased to command
proposed.ja: 恩恵をもって命じ給うた

terms.gloss: Komsomol, the Communist youth league; the director's shouted pose for the girl on camera
terms.why_hard: Komsomol should be a fixed proper noun across the book, not paraphrased

proposed.ja: コムソモールからのご挨拶！

terms.gloss: Horse-drawn cab and its driver, still the ordinary urban transport in 1927
terms.why_hard: Not a taxi; the trams-versus-cabs contrast is the chapter's point

proposed.ja: 辻馬車

terms.gloss: Stargorod lane where Polesov and the fortune-teller live (house No. 5)
terms.why_hard: One transliteration for the street throughout; 'переулок' rendered as lane consistently

proposed.ja: ペレレシンスキー横丁

conventions: Dialogue: keep the Russian dash in the source line; en uses double quotes, zh uses “ ”, ja uses 「 」; narrator's mock-solemn asides stay in the same register with no added exclamation.

Names: keep name + patronymic wherever the Russian has it; en transliteration BGN-style (Vorobyaninov, Matveyevich), zh via standard Xinhua tables with ·, ja katakana with ・; do not add -san in ja to Russian name-patronymic forms.

Address: 'господин' (Polesov, pre-revolutionary) → en 'Mister', zh '先生', ja '様'; 'товарищ' → en 'Comrade', zh '同志', ja '同志'; ты/вы shifts are shown in ja by plain vs です・ます style, in en/zh by tone only.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: The young con man; on these pages also 'инспектор пожарной охраны', 'технический директор и главный руководитель концессии', 'главный концессионер'.
terms.why_hard: Name must be fixed once (Ostap, not Ostáp/Ostapp); his mock-official self-titles must be rendered as consistent running epithets, not paraphrased away.

proposed.ja: オスタップ・ベンデル

terms.gloss: Former marshal of the nobility, Bender's partner; the narrator alternates surname, name+patronymic and 'предводитель'.
terms.why_hard: Patronymic must not be dropped or turned into a middle initial; transliteration must be stable (Matveyevich vs Matveevich) across the book.

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇·沃罗比亚尼诺夫
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ・ヴォロビャーニノフ

terms.gloss: Short for предводитель дворянства, the elected marshal of a district's nobility; the narrator uses it as Vorobyaninov's standing epithet.
terms.why_hard: Literal 'leader' or 'ringleader' loses the pre-revolutionary rank and the joke of a marshal of the nobility kicking a priest.

proposed.ja: 貴族団長

terms.gloss: Priest of the church of Frol and Lavr, rival treasure-hunter; also 'батюшка', 'святой отец', 'духовная особа'.
terms.why_hard: Three different address forms carry three tones (affectionate, sarcastic, mock-solemn); collapsing them to 'Father' everywhere kills the sarcasm of 'святой отец'.

proposed.en: Father Fyodor Vostrikov (батюшка: Father; святой отец: holy father; духовная особа: the reverend gentleman)
proposed.zh: 费奥多尔神父·沃斯特里科夫（батюшка：神父；святой отец：圣父；духовная особа：这位神职人士）
proposed.ja: フョードル・ヴォストリコフ神父（батюшка：神父さま；святой отец：聖なる父よ；духовная особа：聖職者殿）

terms.gloss: Manager of the old-age home, the 'bashful thief' of chapter 8; 'Альхен' is a diminutive of Alexander.
terms.why_hard: The diminutive must be kept as a nickname, not normalised to Alexander; the chapter epithet 'голубой' means bashful/shy, not 'gay'.

proposed.zh: 阿利欣（亚历山大·雅科夫列维奇）
proposed.ja: アリヘン（アレクサンドル・ヤコヴレヴィチ）

terms.gloss: Alkhen's freeloading relative who steals the chair; an old woman mangles his patronymic to 'Мелентьевич'.
terms.why_hard: The mangled patronymic is a deliberate joke and must be preserved as a different name, not silently corrected.

proposed.zh: 帕沙·埃米利耶维奇 / 帕什卡·梅连季耶维奇
proposed.ja: パーシャ・エミリエヴィチ / パーシカ・メレンチエヴィチ

terms.gloss: Alkhen's wife's brothers, all with the patronymic Yakovlevich, lodged and fed at the home; 'уцелевшие Яковлевичи' is a running gag.
terms.why_hard: The plural patronymic used as a family label needs a fixed device ('the Yakovleviches'); losing it loses the joke about a whole clan on state porridge.

proposed.zh: 雅科夫列维奇们（未成年的伊西多尔·雅科夫列维奇）
proposed.ja: ヤコヴレヴィチ一党（未成年のイシドル・ヤコヴレヴィチ）

terms.gloss: The Stargorod Social Security Department's Old-Age Home No. 2, the 'богадельня' where Ostap poses as fire inspector.
terms.why_hard: The acronym Старсобес (Старгородский отдел социального обеспечения) must be unpacked once and reused; leaving 'Starsobes' opaque or calling it a 'nursing home' misleads.

proposed.zh: 斯塔尔戈罗德社会保障局第二养老院
proposed.ja: スタルゴロド社会保障局第二養老院

terms.gloss: The 'red corner': a room in every Soviet workplace or dormitory for political posters, newspapers and meetings.
terms.why_hard: Literal 'red corner' reads as decor; needs the one-time note that it is the agitprop room, then a fixed term.

proposed.ja: 赤いコーナー（政治学習室）

terms.gloss: A foam fire extinguisher, brand 'Eclair', that 'sings' throughout chapter 8 and finally erupts.
terms.why_hard: The mock-technical compound 'пеногон' must sound like a product label, and the brand name must stay consistent so the running gag lands.

proposed.ja: 泡消火器「エクレール」

terms.gloss: Antonina Nezhdanova, celebrated Bolshoi soprano, one of the first to hold the title People's Artist of the Republic.
terms.why_hard: The title must be rendered as an official Soviet honorific, and the reader needs to know she is a famous coloratura for the top-F joke to work.

proposed.en: People's Artist of the Republic Nezhdanova (the soprano)
proposed.zh: 共和国人民演员涅日丹诺娃（女高音歌唱家）
proposed.ja: 共和国人民芸術家ネジダーノワ（ソプラノ歌手）

terms.gloss: Made of or coloured like toile-du-Nord, a cheap grey-blue cotton; the old women's uniform fabric in chapter 8, here a cook's cap and the extinguisher foam.
terms.why_hard: Transliterating 'tualdenor' is meaningless; the colour must be named the same way each time since the narrator keeps reusing it as a joke.

proposed.ja: 灰色木綿（トワル・デュ・ノール）の

terms.gloss: Ostap addresses the old women as 'maidens/girls'; a recurring deadpan mock-gallantry.
terms.why_hard: Must be the same word each time and read as ironic gallantry, not literal description of age.

proposed.zh: 姑娘们（“可悲啊，姑娘们” / “安静点，姑娘们”）
proposed.ja: お嬢さん方（「悲しいことですな、お嬢さん方」／「落ち着いて、お嬢さん方」）

terms.gloss: ДОПР, дом принудительных работ: a 1920s forced-labour prison (Ukrainian SSR term); 'пошел в монахи — сидит в допре' is a prison joke.
terms.why_hard: Must be a prison, not a 'workhouse' or 'monastery'; the reader needs the monk/prison pun to survive.

proposed.ja: 強制労働所（刑務所）

terms.gloss: Ostap's excuse for not hitting Pasha: 'Zarathustra does not permit it', a mock-Nietzschean scruple.
terms.why_hard: Must keep Nietzsche's Zarathustra recognisable (not Zoroaster the prophet) and keep the deadpan tone.

proposed.ja: ツァラトゥストラが許さん

terms.gloss: Ostap's insult: 'abortion victim', i.e. a botched, unwanted specimen of humanity.
terms.why_hard: Literal rendering reads as an accusation about the victim's mother; needs a fixed comic insult that keeps the abortion image.

proposed.ja: この堕胎のし損ないめ

terms.gloss: Ostap misuses nautical jargon: 'cast off the lines, but don't shove off', i.e. stay put.
terms.why_hard: Rendering as plain 'stay here' loses the sailor-talk register that is Ostap's signature; the internal contradiction is the joke.

proposed.en: cast off, but don't shove off
proposed.ja: 綱は解け、だが船は出すな

terms.gloss: Article 114 of the 1926 RSFSR Criminal Code, which Ostap cites (bribing an official) while pocketing the bribe.
terms.why_hard: Keep the number and the mock-legal formula intact; do not 'correct' the article to a modern code.

proposed.ja: 刑法第百十四条

terms.gloss: A ten-ruble note of the 1922-47 gold-backed currency, a substantial bribe.
terms.why_hard: 'Ten rubles' loses the period flavour, 'chervonets' alone is opaque; fix one hybrid rendering for the whole book.

proposed.ja: 十ルーブル金券（チェルヴォーネツ）

terms.gloss: Ostap's catchphrase 'the session continues', echoing the parliamentary formula after an assassination attempt; it became a Russian proverb.
terms.why_hard: Must be one fixed formula every time Ostap says it (it recurs across the novel) and sound like an official minute, not casual speech.

proposed.ja: 会議は続行する！

terms.gloss: Fictional provincial town ('Old Town') where the first part is set; also in the compounds Старсобес, Старгико, губплан.
terms.why_hard: Never translate as 'Old Town'; transliterate once and keep the same base in all acronyms.

proposed.ja: スタルゴロド

terms.gloss: Soviet acronym institutions: provincial planning commission, mill-construction trust, a Stargorod cooperative or communal-services body.
terms.why_hard: Acronyms are part of the period colour; the translator must choose one policy (transliterate + gloss vs. expand) and apply it to every acronym in the book.

proposed.en: the Gubplan (provincial planning board) / Melstroi (mill-construction trust) / Stargiko
proposed.zh: 省计划委员会 / 磨坊建设托拉斯 / 斯塔尔戈罗德合作社
proposed.ja: 県計画委員会 / 製粉建設トラスト / スタルゴロド協同組合

terms.gloss: 'Lena Events Street', a Soviet renaming after the 1912 Lena goldfields massacre; paired with 'улица Маркса и Энгельса' and 'Большая Пушкинская'.
terms.why_hard: Not the Lena river as scenery: the street name commemorates a massacre and is a joke about revolutionary renaming; keep all street names in one style.

proposed.ja: レナ事件通り

terms.gloss: A chair by Gambs, the Petersburg court furniture firm; the twelve treasure chairs of the title, walnut with bent legs and English chintz.
terms.why_hard: The maker's name must be stable (Gambs, not Hambs/Gamps) since the whole book hunts 'Gambs chairs'.

proposed.ja: ガンブス製の椅子

terms.gloss: The municipal housing department (жилищный отдел) that Vorobyaninov is sent to trace the chairs.
terms.why_hard: Must be one fixed rendering as an office name, not 'housing office' one time and 'residential department' the next.

proposed.ja: 住宅課

terms.gloss: Church of Sts Florus and Laurus, patrons of horses, in the folk name forms Frol and Lavr.
terms.why_hard: Choose once between the Latin saints and the Russian folk forms; the folk forms carry the provincial flavour.

proposed.en: the church of St Frol and St Lavr
proposed.ja: フロルとラヴル教会

terms.gloss: A member of the Soviet militia, i.e. the ordinary police.
terms.why_hard: 'Militiaman' vs 'policeman' must be decided once; 'militia' can wrongly suggest paramilitaries to the target reader.

proposed.ja: 民警

terms.gloss: Wrestling term 'par terre' (ground fighting) applied to two men rolling on rubble; not the theatre stalls.
terms.why_hard: The false-friend 'партер' as 'orchestra seats' would make nonsense; keep the sports-commentary register.

proposed.en: the bout continued on the mat
proposed.ja: 闘いはグラウンドに移った

terms.gloss: 'Only horns and legs were left', from the nursery song about the grey goat; means utterly destroyed (echoed later in Ilf & Petrov's 'Рога и копыта').
terms.why_hard: A literal rendering leaves the reader thinking the chair had horns; needs a fixed idiomatic equivalent that keeps the comic image.

proposed.en: nothing left but the horns and the hooves
proposed.ja: 残ったのは角と脚だけ

terms.gloss: A 1920s foxtrot/shimmy hit whose lyric mentions camels and the Botocudos ('ба-та-ку-ды'); Ostap hums it.
terms.why_hard: Verse must be rendered as singable doggerel, and 'ба-та-ку-ды' identified as the Botocudo tribe, not a nonsense word.

proposed.en: 'Shimmy' (Once it was the camels did it, / once the Bo-to-cu-dos shook it, / now the whole wide world is dancing shimmy…)
proposed.zh: 《西迷舞》（从前是骆驼这么跳，/ 从前博托库多人这么跳，/ 如今全世界都跳西迷舞……）
proposed.ja: 『シミー』（昔はラクダがやっていた、/ 昔はボトクード族が踊っていた、/ 今じゃ世界中がシミーを踊る……）

terms.gloss: A newsboy's cry mangling Izvestia, plus the satirical weekly Smekhach and the illustrated Krasnaya Niva.
terms.why_hard: The mispronunciation must be reproduced, and the titles kept as real recognisable periodicals rather than translated descriptively.

proposed.en: Moscow paper Izvestya! Smekhach! Krasnaya Niva!
proposed.zh: 莫斯科报纸《消息报》、《笑匙》杂志、《红色田野》！
proposed.ja: モスクワの新聞『ズヴェスチヤ』、雑誌『スメハーチ』、『赤い畑』！

conventions: Dialogue: replace the Russian speech dash with target-language quotation marks (en “ ”, zh “ ”, ja 「 」); keep the narrator's interjected stage directions as separate clauses.

Names: always give name + patronymic where the Russian does, transliterated once per person (en: Ippolit Matveyevich; zh: 新华社-style transliteration with ·; ja: katakana with long vowels), and preserve deliberate mangling such as Пашка Мелентьевич.

Register: render pre-revolutionary -с (да-с) as an obsequious tag (en 'yes, sir'; zh '是的，先生'; ja 'ですとも'); mark Ostap's switch from вы to ты toward Pasha by blunter address in en/zh and by dropping honorifics (お前, plain form) in ja.

value.term: «Большевики пишут письмо Чемберлену» / «Запорожцы пишут письмо султану»
value.finding: In ch. 5 Bender considers offering the Stargorod children's commission (Стардеткомиссия) the rights to a still-unpainted picture, 'The Bolsheviks Write a Letter to Chamberlain', modelled on Repin's 'Zaporozhian Cossacks Write a Letter to the Sultan' (Russian Museum, 1880–91; English title 'Reply of the Zaporozhian Cossacks'), which every Russian knew: a crowd of laughing Cossacks dictating an obscene refusal to the Turkish sultan's demand of submission. The joke is topical: on 23 Feb 1927 British Foreign Secretary Austen Chamberlain sent a note demanding the USSR stop anti-British propaganda; Pravda answered with 'Our answer to Chamberlain' (2 Mar 1927), Britain broke off relations in May after the ARCOS raid, and the slogan became a nationwide poster/fund-raising campaign (Osoaviakhim air squadron 'Our answer to Chamberlain'), so Chamberlain was the stock villain of 1927 cartoons. Bender's idea is even second-hand: Krasny Perets no. 6 (1923) had already printed 'The Bolsheviks Write a Reply to the English Curzon' with Kalinin, Chicherin, Trotsky, Stalin etc. in the Cossacks' poses. Kalinin (head of state, 'all-Union elder') and Chicherin (foreign commissar) are the leaders whose costumes Bender worries about; the phrase 'наш ответ Чемберлену' survives in Russian as an ironic idiom for a blustering 'worthy reply'. The Richardson English translation renders it 'The Bolsheviks Answer Chamberlain' after 'The Zaporozhe Cossacks Answer the Sultan'.

value.finding: Bortniansky's hymn (1794, words by Kheraskov, after a psalm), used as the unofficial state anthem of the Russian Empire before 'Боже, Царя храни' (1833), and thereafter still the tune the Kremlin's Spasskaya Tower chimes played from 1856 until October 1917; it was then the official hymn of the White armies (1918–23) and of the émigré community. For a Soviet reader in 1928 it was therefore not a random church piece but the sound of the old regime and the Whites, which is why a NEP-era fire extinguisher 'Эклер' hissing this melody (Chapter VIII, the old women's home) is a joke of misplaced loyalties. Sources give no Soviet ban, but the association with tsarism and emigration was live. Established renderings: English 'How Glorious Is Our Lord in Zion' (en.wikipedia, recordings); Chinese 吾主在锡安是何等光荣 (zh.wikipedia article title); Japanese has no article of its own — the Bortniansky page uses the transliteration 『コリ・スラーヴェン』 and Russia Beyond uses 「シオンのわれらが主の何と輝かしき」. The prompt's mention of Durov/VKontakte and '2013' does not apply; the book is 1928.

value.finding: «Быстроупак» is a fictional private packing office in Stargorod: in chapter X it 'announces itself to respected citizen-customers with a black sign with round gold letters' next to the bagel artel, its 'молодцы' (toughs) help the militiaman and later queue for flour, and in chapter XIV its owner Дядьев, a former textile merchant and NEP businessman, is fleeced by Bender's 'Union of the Sword and Ploughshare'. The name is a mock Soviet-style clipped compound (быстро + упаковка), the same pattern as real 1920s abbreviations (Хлебопродукт, Москвошвея), and Ilf recorded it in his 1927 notebook simply as 'Упаковочная контора «Быстроупак»' alongside 'Пивная «Вавилон»', i.e. as a specimen of absurd NEP-era shop names. For a Russian reader it connotes a small private nepman firm dressed in bureaucratic-sounding branding; it is not a proverbial phrase. John Richardson's English translation (1961, the standard text online) renders it 'Fastpack' throughout ('the Fastpack packing office', 'young toughs from Fastpack', 'Dyadyev, owner of Fastpack'). Search did not surface the Chinese (张佩文 2004; 白桦熊 2022) or Japanese (江川卓 1969) renderings; those are not verified.

value.finding: Огонёк (literally 'little flame/light') is a real Moscow illustrated weekly: founded in St Petersburg on 21 December 1899 as a supplement to Birzhevye vedomosti, closed in 1918, and revived in Moscow on 1 April 1923 by the journalist Mikhail Koltsov as 'a Soviet magazine with the old name'. In the NEP years it was the mass-market general-interest picture weekly (photo essays, popular science, celebrities; circulation reportedly around half a million by 1925), which is exactly why a provincial barber in Stargorod would keep it on his table and mine it for 'medical' facts. Ilf and Petrov themselves later wrote for it, so the joke is affectionate: the magazine stands for cheap urban modernity as digested in the provinces. It became a perestroika icon under Korotich (4.6 million copies in 1990), passed to Kommersant in 2009, and ceased print in December 2020; a reader in 2013 knew it as a still-running, slightly old-fashioned national institution. The novel's passage (Part I, ch. 2) is rendered by John Richardson as 'the Moscow magazine Ogonyok'; Chinese coverage uses 《星火》 (zh.wikipedia, Russia Beyond Chinese); Japanese uses katakana オゴニョーク (ja.wikipedia, Russia Beyond Japanese, Kotobank). The prompt's reference to Durov/VKontakte does not apply to this term.

value.finding: Bortniansky's hymn (1794, words by Kheraskov, after a psalm), used as the unofficial state anthem of the Russian Empire before 'Боже, Царя храни' (1833), and thereafter still the tune the Kremlin's Spasskaya Tower chimes played from 1856 until October 1917; it was then the official hymn of the White armies (1918–23) and of the émigré community. For a Soviet reader in 1928 it was therefore not a random church piece but the sound of the old regime and the Whites, which is why a NEP-era fire extinguisher 'Эклер' hissing this melody (Chapter VIII, the old women's home) is a joke of misplaced loyalties. Sources give no Soviet ban, but the association with tsarism and emigration was live. Established renderings: English 'How Glorious Is Our Lord in Zion' (en.wikipedia, recordings); Chinese 吾主在锡安是何等光荣 (zh.wikipedia article title); Japanese has no article of its own — the Bortniansky page uses the transliteration 『コリ・スラーヴェン』 and Russia Beyond uses 「シオンのわれらが主の何と輝かしき」. The prompt's mention of Durov/VKontakte and '2013' does not apply; the book is 1928.

value.finding: Огонёк (literally 'little flame/light') is a real Moscow illustrated weekly: founded in St Petersburg on 21 December 1899 as a supplement to Birzhevye vedomosti, closed in 1918, and revived in Moscow on 1 April 1923 by the journalist Mikhail Koltsov as 'a Soviet magazine with the old name'. In the NEP years it was the mass-market general-interest picture weekly (photo essays, popular science, celebrities; circulation reportedly around half a million by 1925), which is exactly why a provincial barber in Stargorod would keep it on his table and mine it for 'medical' facts. Ilf and Petrov themselves later wrote for it, so the joke is affectionate: the magazine stands for cheap urban modernity as digested in the provinces. It became a perestroika icon under Korotich (4.6 million copies in 1990), passed to Kommersant in 2009, and ceased print in December 2020; a reader in 2013 knew it as a still-running, slightly old-fashioned national institution. The novel's passage (Part I, ch. 2) is rendered by John Richardson as 'the Moscow magazine Ogonyok'; Chinese coverage uses 《星火》 (zh.wikipedia, Russia Beyond Chinese); Japanese uses katakana オゴニョーク (ja.wikipedia, Russia Beyond Japanese, Kotobank). The prompt's reference to Durov/VKontakte does not apply to this term.

value.finding: It is the coffin-maker Bezenchuk's signature filler-oath in chapter 1 of The Twelve Chairs (1928): 'туды' is sub-standard for 'туда' (thither), and the whole thing is a euphemised regional curse of the 'туды твою мать' family with the obscene noun swapped for the absurd 'качель' (swing; dialect 'качалка'). The Big Dictionary of Russian Sayings (Mokienko & Nikitina 2003, citing Podyukov 1989) lists 'туды (растуды) твою/вашу/его качель!' as prost., obl., bran.: a curse ('may you perish') or an expression of extreme annoyance; Russian readers today know it almost entirely through Bezenchuk and quote it as a jokey 'to hell with it', with folk accounts saying Ilf and Petrov picked it up from yard-keepers' or Odessa speech. John Richardson's 1961 English translation flattens it to a recurring 'durn it' ('Does the Nymph, durn it, really give good service?'); Anne Fisher's 2011 translation could not be checked, and no Chinese (Zhang Peiwen 2004, Xu Changhan 2022) or Japanese (Egawa Taku 1966/69) rendering was found online. The brief's mention of Durov, VKontakte and 2013 is template noise and does not apply to this term.

value.finding: A milítsioner is a rank-and-file officer of the milítsiya, the Soviet civil police. The name was adopted by the Provisional Government's decree of 17 April 1917 and reaffirmed by the Bolsheviks on 10 November 1917 as the 'Workers' and Peasants' Militsiya', deliberately chosen to tie the new force to popular self-organisation and to disown the tsarist 'politsiya'; the word survived until Russia restored 'politsiya' on 1 March 2011. In 1928 it therefore carried a distinctly new-regime flavour: a milítsioner is the ordinary street cop of NEP Russia, a figure of mild comedy rather than fear (the terror organs were the OGPU, not the militsiya), and the narrators use him as a stock piece of Soviet street furniture. John Richardson's English translation (the widely circulated 1961/1965 text) renders the institution as 'the Soviet militia' in explicit contrast to 'the tsarist police'; Japanese reference usage is 民警 (ミリツィヤ) for the Soviet-era force versus 警察 for post-2011; Chinese Wikipedia titles the force 苏联民兵 but records 民警 as the standard alternative, and in Chinese everyday usage 民警 also denotes an ordinary uniformed officer of the PRC's 人民警察, which makes it read naturally. The prompt's references to 2013, Durov and VKontakte do not apply to this 1928 term and were disregarded.

value.finding: Жилотдел is the standard early-Soviet abbreviation of жилищный отдел, the housing department attached to the executive committee of a local Soviet; dictionaries of Soviet usage define it as the office that 'kept account of and distributed living space' (учёт и распределение жилой площади). In 1918–1921 these departments (and their district housing councils/commissions) carried out the requisition of 'bourgeois' flats and movable property under decrees such as the Moscow Soviet's 11 Sept 1918 order 'О порядке реквизиции жилых помещений и движимого имущества', issuing the ордера (allocation warrants) by which rooms and furniture were assigned — the very papers Ostap buys from Korobeinikov. In the novel the term is concrete and load-bearing: all Vorobyaninov's furniture 'в 1919 году увезли в жилотдел' (ch. VII); the building 'раньше была здесь женская гимназия, а потом жилотдел' (ch. X); 'жилотдел был расформирован в 1921 году и... обширный его архив слит с архивом Старкомхоза' (ch. XI); one chair went to Gritsatsuev 'по резолюции завжилотделом т. Буркина'. For a 1928 (and still a 2013) Russian reader it connotes War-Communism confiscation and уплотнение, a dead institution whose paperwork outlived it, and the deadpan officialese of the ордер. Existing renderings: Richardson's English (lib.ru) uses 'the housing division' throughout and 'Stargorod communal services' for Старкомхоз; Fisher's 2011 text could not be checked online; a Chinese retelling of the plot uses 住宅管理科 for the 1919 confiscation, and Xu Changhan's 2022 translation and Egawa Taku's 1969 Japanese translation (十二の椅子, 筑摩書房) exist but their wording for this term was not retrievable, so no established zh/ja rendering is confirmed.
sources: https://www.amazon.co.jp/十二の椅子-1969年-イリヤ・イリフ/dp/B000J94TF4

value.finding: In chapter I of the novel the phrase names the parish of Father Fyodor Vostrikov: 'священник церкви Фрола и Лавра, отец Федор', in the county town of N (Stargorod). Flor and Lavr (Latin Florus and Laurus) are 2nd-century Illyrian martyr-stonemasons whose feast (18/31 August) became the Russian peasant 'horse holiday'; in folk speech and church dedications they are Frol and Lavr (or Lavyor), the 'лошадники', and hundreds of provincial Russian churches bore the name. For a Russian reader Fyodor's parish is thus an ordinary small-town church with a homely, peasant, faintly comic dedication (Frol is the colloquial form that displaced Flor), which matches the priest's greedy, provincial character. English translators split: Richardson (1961) has 'the Church of St. Frol and St. Laurence'; the Fisher (2011) edition and current English coverage use 'Frol and Lavr Church'. Chinese and Japanese book renderings could not be verified online; the 2022 Shanghai Yiwen preview appears to give 弗罗尔与拉夫尔教堂, and Japanese coverage of the saints themselves uses フロルスとラウルス.

value.finding: Klavdia Ivanovna Petukhova is Ippolit Matveevich Vorobyaninov's тёща (his late wife Marie's mother), an old provincial noblewoman in Stargorod who dies in chapter II ('Кончина мадам Петуховой') after confessing that she sewed her diamonds into the seat of one of the twelve dining-room chairs; the novel's Part Three is titled 'Сокровище мадам Петуховой'. Chapter I gives her the book's deadpan treatment: 'Ипполит Матвеевич не любил своей тещи. Клавдия Ивановна была глупа... Скупа она была до чрезвычайности... Голос у ней был такой силы и густоты, что ему позавидовал бы Ричард Львиное Сердце', and she is a dreamer of prophetic dreams. The text calls her only 'Клавдия Ивановна', 'теща', 'старуха' or 'мадам Петухова'; the name-plus-patronymic is the ordinary respectful Russian address for an older woman and carries no joke of its own — the comedy is in the narration around her. For a Russian reader she is the stock тёща of Soviet humour (the domineering mother-in-law who knows the family money) and the origin of the whole treasure hunt. The 1961 Richardson English translation (lib.ru) anglicises her as 'Claudia Ivanovna' and uses 'mother-in-law' throughout; a search summary claimed Fisher (2011) does the same but this could not be verified. The 2022 上海译文 Chinese edition (白桦熊) titles chapter II '佩图霍娃太太辞世'; 克拉夫季娅 is the 新华社 standard Chinese for Клавдия. No Japanese source giving the katakana of her name was found (Egawa Takashi's 1966/1969 translation is not online); Japanese summaries call her 義母.

value.finding: Klavdia Ivanovna Petukhova is Ippolit Matveevich Vorobyaninov's тёща (his late wife Marie's mother), an old provincial noblewoman in Stargorod who dies in chapter II ('Кончина мадам Петуховой') after confessing that she sewed her diamonds into the seat of one of the twelve dining-room chairs; the novel's Part Three is titled 'Сокровище мадам Петуховой'. Chapter I gives her the book's deadpan treatment: 'Ипполит Матвеевич не любил своей тещи. Клавдия Ивановна была глупа... Скупа она была до чрезвычайности... Голос у ней был такой силы и густоты, что ему позавидовал бы Ричард Львиное Сердце', and she is a dreamer of prophetic dreams. The text calls her only 'Клавдия Ивановна', 'теща', 'старуха' or 'мадам Петухова'; the name-plus-patronymic is the ordinary respectful Russian address for an older woman and carries no joke of its own — the comedy is in the narration around her. For a Russian reader she is the stock тёща of Soviet humour (the domineering mother-in-law who knows the family money) and the origin of the whole treasure hunt. The 1961 Richardson English translation (lib.ru) anglicises her as 'Claudia Ivanovna' and uses 'mother-in-law' throughout; a search summary claimed Fisher (2011) does the same but this could not be verified. The 2022 上海译文 Chinese edition (白桦熊) titles chapter II '佩图霍娃太太辞世'; 克拉夫季娅 is the 新华社 standard Chinese for Клавдия. No Japanese source giving the katakana of her name was found (Egawa Takashi's 1966/1969 translation is not online); Japanese summaries call her 義母.

value.finding: «Треугольник» is the Petersburg rubber works on the Obvodny Canal, founded 1859/60 as the Russian-American Rubber Manufactory (ТРАРМ); from 1888 it stamped its galoshes with a triangle so that illiterate buyers could recognise them, took the trade name «Треугольник» officially in 1908, and was renamed «Красный треугольник» after nationalisation (1922). It was the country's near-monopoly galosh maker, supplier to the Imperial court, and in the NEP years the rubber trust advertised heavily (Mayakovsky wrote its slogans), so for a 1928 reader the word meant one thing: galoshes. In ch. XI the swindled archivist Korobeinikov kicks his table and «подпрыгивала пепельница, сделанная на манер калоши с красной надписью «Треугольник»» — a promotional galosh-shaped ashtray, a pun on the firm's product that also fits the petty-bourgeois clutter of his room; the same brand recurs as torn «Треугольник» tyre covers in Bezenchuk's town. Richardson's English (1961) renders it plainly as 'Triangle' ('the clog-shaped ash-tray with the word "Triangle" on it', misreading калоша as clog); English sources on the factory use 'Triangle'/'Red Triangle'. I found no published Chinese or Japanese rendering of this sentence online (the prompt's mention of Durov/VKontakte/2013 is a template slip unrelated to this 1928 term).

value.finding: Старгород (Star-gorod, literally 'Old Town') is the fictional provincial town where Part One, «Старгородский лев», is set; its people are старгородцы and its institutions carry the adjective старгородский (Старгородская правда, the 1 May tram line). Ilf and Petrov borrowed the name from Leskov's «Соборяне» (1872), where Stargorod embodies patriarchal old Russia; in the 1928 novel the same name is turned ironic, standing for provincial bustle and NEP-era pretension in a town of pre-revolutionary leftovers. Its real-life prototype is generally held to be Starobelsk (Luhansk region), which the authors visited as Gudok correspondents in 1923; the village Chmarovka from which Ostap arrives is a real Starobelsk suburb. Established renderings: English translations (Richardson 1961, Fisher 2011) use 'Stargorod'; Ekawa Takashi's Japanese translation uses スタルゴロド; but the Chinese tradition (Xu Changhan; Bai Huaxiong, Shanghai Translation 2022) calques it as 老城 (Part One: 老城里的狮子), and I found no Chinese edition using a transliteration.

value.finding: A fictional character, not a real person: the Stargorod mechanic of The Twelve Chairs, introduced in the chapter «Слесарь, попугай и гадалка» as «слесарь-интеллигент» and, among the town's «кустари с мотором», the most inept — the narrators' verdict «Это был кипучий лентяй» (Richardson 1961: 'an ebullient idler'). His workshop is full of unfinished jobs; he chatters with the fortune-teller Elena Stanislavovna, longs for the old regime, and Ostap recruits him as the first dupe of the bogus 'Union of the Sword and Ploughshare'. For a Russian reader by 2013 he is a stock type — the loud know-it-all bungler — and «кипучий лентяй» is itself a proverbial phrase. The text calls him by surname, by 'Виктор Михайлович' (the polite form, often with mock solemnity) and by 'слесарь'; all three refer to the same man. The two English translations already differ on the first name (Richardson: 'Victor Mikhailovich Polesov'; modern usage and the Fisher-era coverage: 'Viktor'). No attested Chinese or Japanese spelling of the full name was found online; a Chinese reading edition refers to him as 波列索夫, a 钳工.

value.finding: Елена Станиславовна Боур is a minor character of the Stargorod chapters: in 1899 she was the young wife of the new district prosecutor Bour, whom Vorobyaninov carried off to Paris (the cut chapter «Прошлое регистратора загса» gives the back-story); by 1927 she is a shabby, ageing widow in Pereleshinsky Lane who lives by laying out cards (a king of clubs on her heart, a queen of diamonds beside him) with a white parrot in red underpants for company, and whose flat hosts Ostap's fake monarchist cell, the «Союз меча и орала». The chapter title «Слесарь, попугай и гадалка» fixes her label: гадалка is the ordinary, slightly disreputable NEP-era word for a woman who reads cards for money, not a witch or a mystic, and the joke is the fallen 'prokurorsha' who still forgets she has no servants. Her patronymic Stanislavovna (and the surname Bour) marks her as of Polish or foreign-Catholic stock, a common type in the old provincial gentry; Russian readers register this without comment, so it needs no gloss. Published renderings: Richardson (1961) and Fisher (Northwestern) use 'Elena Stanislavovna' and 'fortune-teller' ('The Mechanic, the Parrot, and the Fortune-teller'); the 2022 Shanghai Translation edition titles the chapter 「钳工、鹦鹉和算命婆」; the 张佩文 2004 edition is reported to use 叶列娜·斯塔尼斯拉沃芙娜. No Japanese wording from 江川卓's 1969 translation could be verified online.

value.finding: A stern placard on the wall of the Stargorod ZAGS (registry office) in chapter I, where Ippolit Matveyevich registers marriages and deaths; it hangs under the wheezing clock and so cows the young groom that, 'although he had not yet begun his business, he already wanted to leave' (Хотя дела своего мужчина в пиджаке еще и не начинал, но уйти ему уже хотелось), before blurting out 'Сочетаться!'. Dushenko's Большой словарь цитат identifies it as a slightly altered version of a real 1920s institutional placard, «Кончил дело — уходи», one of the curt anti-loitering notices (alongside «Без дела не входить», «Соблюдай очередь») that Soviet offices hung for petitioners; Ilf and Petrov reused the wording as the title of a 1932 feuilleton mocking the anonymous author of such 'комхозовские афоризмы'. For a Russian reader it is the voice of NEP-era bureaucratic rudeness, and via the novel it became a catchphrase. Established renderings found: Richardson (1961) 'Finish Your Business and Leave'; the Shanghai Translation (2022, tr. 白桦熊) text surfaced in search as '事情办完——即刻走人' (page itself could not be fetched to confirm); no Japanese wording from Egawa Takashi's translation was findable online.

value.note_for_reader: A real Soviet office placard of the 1920s (originally «Кончил дело — уходи», 'Done? Then go'), hung to stop petitioners lingering.
value.rationale: Each rendering keeps the denotation and the flat imperative notice register (English matches Richardson's established wording; Chinese follows the 2022 Shanghai Translation reading with the original's dash; Japanese uses the 〜こと notice form) and keeps the words the joke needs — business/leave, 事/走, 用/帰る — so the groom's line can echo the placard verbatim; what is lost is the Russian reader's instant recognition of a familiar wall-sign, which the note supplies.

value.finding: A subbotnik (from суббота, Saturday) is a day of unpaid collective labour: the first was held on 12 April 1919 by fifteen communists at the Moscow-Kazan railway depot, who worked through the night repairing locomotives; Lenin blessed the practice in 'A Great Beginning' (Pravda, 28 June 1919) as 'the actual beginning of communism', and himself carried logs at the first all-Russian subbotnik in the Kremlin on 1 May 1920. By the NEP years the word already carried a double charge: official heroism-of-labour rhetoric on one side, and on the other the weary, half-ironic memory of mass mobilisations with brass bands that produced little (encyclopedia.com calls them 'a mixture of socialist idealism and coercion'; Russian Life notes that once the fervour faded they became institutionalised and mandatory). This is exactly how the novel uses it: in ch. XIII ('Дышите глубже, вы взволнованы!') the engineer Treukhov recalls that 'в двадцатом году, когда начались субботники, деповцы и канатчики пошли с музыкой на Гусище и весь день копали какие-то ямы' -- holes dug in the wrong place that had to be filled in again -- and later, on the tram-opening platform, 'хотел сказать многое. И про субботники, и про тяжелую работу'. The established renderings are 'subbotnik(s)' in English (Wikipedia, Encyclopedia.com, Russian Life, Marxists.org all keep the loanword), 星期六义务劳动 in Chinese (Baidu Baike lists 共产主义星期六义务劳动 with short form 星期六义务劳动; it is also the everyday press term for present-day Russian subbotniks), and スボートニク in Japanese, glossed 土曜労働 or 勤労奉仕 (ja.wikipedia, RBTH Japan). I could not obtain the Richardson (1961) or Fisher (2011) wording for this passage online; the lib.ru text fetched only reaches chapter 7. Note: the brief's line about 'Durov and VKontakte ... around 2013' does not apply to this term or this book and was ignored.

rendering.ja: スボートニク（土曜奉仕労働）

value.note_for_reader: Subbotnik (from субботa, 'Saturday'): unpaid collective 'volunteer' labour days launched in 1919 and championed by Lenin as the seed of communism; by the 1920s already a byword for bands, banners and holes dug in the wrong place.
value.rationale: All three renderings keep the denotation (unpaid collective labour on a Saturday) and the Soviet-institutional register; English and Japanese also keep the loanword so the reader recognises it on repeat occurrences, with a short in-line gloss the first time and the bare word thereafter. What is given up is the connotation of hollow enthusiasm, which no target-language phrase carries -- the narration's own deadpan detail about the holes supplies it, and the one-line note names it once. Chinese binds the standard press/encyclopedia term rather than a transliteration because it is instantly readable and already established; the 义务 ('duty/volunteer') element even keeps a trace of the voluntary-yet-obligatory ambiguity.

XIII ('Дышите глубже, вы взволнованы!') the engineer Treukhov recalls that 'в двадцатом году, когда начались субботники, деповцы и канатчики пошли с музыкой на Гусище и весь день копали какие-то ямы' -- holes dug in the wrong place that had to be filled in again -- and later, on the tram-opening platform, 'хотел сказать многое. The established renderings are 'subbotnik(s)' in English (Wikipedia, Encyclopedia.com, Russian Life, Marxists.org all keep the loanword), 星期六义务劳动 in Chinese (Baidu Baike lists 共产主义星期六义务劳动 with short form 星期六义务劳动; it is also the everyday press term for present-day Russian subbotniks), and スボートニク in Japanese, glossed 土曜労働 or 勤労奉仕 (ja.wikipedia, RBTH Japan). I could not obtain the Richardson (1961) or Fisher (2011) wording for this passage online; the lib.ru text fetched only reaches chapter 7. value.note_for_reader: Subbotnik (from субботa, 'Saturday'): unpaid collective 'volunteer' labour days launched in 1919 and championed by Lenin as the seed of communism; by the 1920s already a byword for bands, banners and holes dug in the wrong place.

value.finding: The unnamed 'district town of N' of the opening chapter (Bezenchuk and the 'Nymph'); the manuscript shows the town was later merged into Stargorod. 'Город N' is a stock fictional toponym of Russian literature for a provincial backwater (Gogol's Revizor and Dead Souls, Chekhov, Turgenev, Dostoevsky), and N is a placeholder variable, not an initial: the forms 'NN' and 'Энск' exist alongside it. 'Уездный' marks the seat of an uezd, the second-level pre-1917 administrative unit (Wiktionary: 'uyezd town, district town, county town'); the Soviet reform of 1923–1929 replaced uezds with raions, so in 1928 the word was already faintly old-regime and provincial. For a Russian reader the phrase signals from the first line 'this is a Gogol/Chekhov provincial nowhere, treated with mock solemnity'. Published renderings: Richardson (1961) 'the regional centre of N.', Fisher (Northwestern, 2011) 'the provincial town of N'; 徐昌翰 (江苏凤凰文艺, 2022) 'N县城'; no Japanese text of 江川卓's translation (筑摩書房 1969 / 集英社 1966) could be verified online.

value.note_for_reader: 'N' is not an initial: since Gogol, Russian fiction calls an anonymous provincial town 'the town of N'; 'district town' (уездный город) was the seat of a pre-revolutionary uezd.
value.rationale: All three keep the bare letter N (the Gogol convention) and a small-town denotation: English 'district town' is the dictionary rendering of уездный город and keeps it distinct from Gogol's 'provincial (губернский) town'; Chinese N县城 is the published rendering and 县 maps uezd well; Japanese N市 follows how Gogol's and Chekhov's N is conventionally rendered but gives up the 'uezd' nuance, since 郡 in Japanese has no town-seat sense and 'N郡の町' misreads N as the district's name. The mock-solemn register is left to the sentence around it.

value.finding: In ch. X Polesov complains that the Stargorod tram has 'четыре мотора «Всеобщей Электрической Компании»' that will just about run, while 'остальные моторы — харьковская работа'. «Всеобщая электрическая компания» is the standard Soviet-era Russian calque of the American General Electric Co.: Lenin's Imperialism (ch. V) uses 'Всеобщая электрич. Ко' for the US trust and 'Всеобщее общество электричества' for its German rival, and AEG's own Russian subsidiary (1901–1918) was named «Всеобщая компания электричества» (ВКЭ), not «электрическая компания». So the phrase denotes GE, and John Richardson's 1961 English translation already renders it 'four General Electric engines'. For a 1928 reader the contrast is imported American quality versus shoddy domestic 'Kharkov work' — with the extra irony, invisible today, that the Kharkov electrical works (later ХЭМЗ) was the former ВКЭ/AEG plant evacuated from Riga in 1915. Fixed corporate names: zh 通用电气公司, ja ゼネラル・エレクトリック (both Wikipedia titles). I could not access the published Chinese (张佩文, 2004) or Japanese (江川卓, 1969) translations of the passage.

value.finding: In Chapter V ('Великий комбинатор') Bender frames the chair hunt as a business deal: 'как непосредственный участник концессии и технический руководитель дела, получаю шестьдесят процентов', and from then on the narrator calls the pair 'концессионеры' and their venture 'концессионное предприятие' (e.g. Chapter XXXIX: 'Повеселевшие концессионеры пошли быстрее'; 'членов-пайщиков концессионного предприятия'). A концессия in 1928 was a precise NEP-era legal institution: under Lenin's decree of 23 Nov 1920 foreign firms (Harriman, Lena Goldfields, German and Japanese companies) got temporary usufruct rights to run state-owned assets for profit; there were 103 such concessions at the 1926 peak and most were annulled by the SNK decree of 27 Dec 1930. To a 1928 reader the word carried newspaper-headline weight: foreign capital, big money, official contracts and a whiff of suspicion; applied to two men chasing chairs it is mock-solemn bureaucratic inflation, and the recurring 60/40 renegotiations keep the joke alive. Both published English translations (Richardson 1961, Fisher 2011) use 'the concessionaires'. I could not verify the exact wording used in the published Chinese (白桦熊, 上海译文 2022) or Japanese (江川卓, 筑摩書房 1969) translations; for the historical institution Chinese sources use 租让/租让制/租让企业 and Japanese sources use 利権 or コンセッション.

value.finding: In the Russian Empire the дворник was the yard-and-street keeper of an apartment house who was also formally enrolled in the police system: after the 1866 attempt on Alexander II dvorniki were made auxiliaries of the MVD, wore a numbered brass badge and carried a whistle to summon the городовой, kept night watch at the gate, registered tenants and their passports, detained beggars and suspicious persons, and served as witnesses at searches, all under the околоточный надзиратель. After 1917 the political and record-keeping side passed to the управдом and housing committee, and the dvornik was left 'with shovel, scraper and broom', but in the NEP 1920s the habit of petty authority over the yard survived, which is exactly the joke in Chapter XIV: the dvornik of house No. 5 whom Polesov calls 'a boor who has got above himself' chases him down the street and beats him while Polesov shouts 'караул!'. In English coverage the word is rendered 'janitor' (Russia Beyond), 'caretaker' (Richardson's 1961 translation), 'street cleaner' (IMDb credits for Tikhon in the 1971 film) and, in Russianist usage, 'yard-keeper'; Fisher's 2011 translation appears to keep 'dvornik', but I could not verify this from the text. I could not verify how the 上海译文 Chinese or the 江川卓 (筑摩書房 1969) Japanese translations render it: the Chinese e-texts were blocked and the Japanese reviews found do not mention Tikhon. 庭番 is the customary rendering in Japanese Dostoevsky translations and 看院人/扫院人 the customary Chinese ones; neither could be confirmed for this book.

value.note_for_reader: A dvornik kept the yard and pavement of an apartment house and, since tsarist times, doubled as the police's man on the block, with badge and whistle; the habit of authority outlived the Revolution.

value.finding: The narrator's mock-heroic standing epithet for Ostap Bender in both novels (chapter 5 of 'Двенадцать стульев' and a chapter of 'Золотой телёнок' bear the title). In 1920s Odessa/NEP speech 'комбинация' meant a clever, usually shady scheme and 'комбинатор' its author (Lechaim traces the formula to Sholem Aleichem's 'человек с комбинациями'); the pompous 'великий' is the authors' irony. It became a proverbial крылатое выражение: dictionaries define it as 'ловкий пройдоха, добивающийся успеха путём сложных операций, уловок, мошенничества', used colloquially with irony or disapproval, and in post-Soviet Russia (a Lenkom production 'Великий комбинатор' opened in the 2010s) it carries as much admiration for resourcefulness as reproach. Existing English translations split: Malamuth 'the great schemer', Richardson 1961 'the smooth operator' (also used in Fisher's presentation of The Little Golden Calf), Gurevich/Anderson 2009 'the grand strategist'; Chinese print translations use 伟大谋士 (张佩文, 人民文学 2004) and 大谋士 (徐昌翰, 江苏凤凰文艺 2022). The Japanese rendering in 江川卓's translation (筑摩書房 1961/1969) could not be verified online; Japanese coverage only paraphrases him as 稀代の詐欺師/ペテン師. The prompt's mention of Durov/VKontakte does not apply to this term.

rendering.ja: 偉大なる策士

value.note_for_reader: Bender's standing epithet, mock-solemn and half-admiring; older English versions say 'the smooth operator'. In Russian it became a byword for a charming schemer.

value.finding: The narrator's mock-heroic standing epithet for Ostap Bender in both novels (chapter 5 of 'Двенадцать стульев' and a chapter of 'Золотой телёнок' bear the title). In 1920s Odessa/NEP speech 'комбинация' meant a clever, usually shady scheme and 'комбинатор' its author (Lechaim traces the formula to Sholem Aleichem's 'человек с комбинациями'); the pompous 'великий' is the authors' irony. It became a proverbial крылатое выражение: dictionaries define it as 'ловкий пройдоха, добивающийся успеха путём сложных операций, уловок, мошенничества', used colloquially with irony or disapproval, and in post-Soviet Russia (a Lenkom production 'Великий комбинатор' opened in the 2010s) it carries as much admiration for resourcefulness as reproach. Existing English translations split: Malamuth 'the great schemer', Richardson 1961 'the smooth operator' (also used in Fisher's presentation of The Little Golden Calf), Gurevich/Anderson 2009 'the grand strategist'; Chinese print translations use 伟大谋士 (张佩文, 人民文学 2004) and 大谋士 (徐昌翰, 江苏凤凰文艺 2022). The Japanese rendering in 江川卓's translation (筑摩書房 1961/1969) could not be verified online; Japanese coverage only paraphrases him as 稀代の詐欺師/ペテン師. The prompt's mention of Durov/VKontakte does not apply to this term.

value.finding: Альхен is the завхоз (supplies manager) of the 2nd Stargorod Social-Security Home (старсобес), a former Vorobyaninov mansion turned old-age home, in chapter VIII 'Голубой воришка'. The text introduces him as Александр Яковлевич; his wife Александра Яковлевна calls him Альхен and he calls her Сашхен — private pet-forms of Alexander/Alexandra, so the nickname must stay a nickname. He is 'застенчивый ворюга': he steals constantly and is constantly ashamed, cheeks burning with embarrassment; the narrator's 'свет не видывал ещё такого голубого воришки' uses голубой in its older sense of innocent, dreamy, idealistic (cf. голубая мечта), and Russian readers' Q&A pages treat it only that way, never in the post-Soviet 'gay' sense — for a 2013 reader the phrase 'голубой воришка' was a proverbial tag for a thief who steals and weeps, fixed by Oleg Tabakov's performance in the 1976 TV film. English translations: Richardson 1961 'Alchen'/'Sashchen', chapter 'The Bashful Chiseller'; Fisher 2011 (Northwestern) 'Alkhen'/'Sashkhen', 'a shy little thief'. The Chinese 张佩文 translation (人民文学 名著名译) renders him 阿尔亨, wife 萨什亨, chapter title 文过饰非的小偷 (other Chinese editions: 知耻无悔的小偷, 温文尔雅的小偷). No online source shows the katakana used in 江川卓's Japanese translation (筑摩書房 1969/1977).

value.finding: Ostap Bender's signature exclamation, first uttered in the chapter «Бриллиантовый дым» (ch. VI in the canonical text): while Vorobyaninov tells the story of the jewels, Ostap keeps jumping up and shouting it 'to the iron stove', then repeats it when they shake hands on the partnership. «Лёд тронулся» is the spring ice-break on a river (ледоход), used figuratively for 'things have finally started moving, the deadlock is over'; «господа присяжные заседатели» is the address a barrister used to the jury in the pre-revolutionary jury court, abolished in 1917, so in 1928 it is a mock-solemn anachronism, Ostap parodying courtroom oratory to give his swindle comic gravitas (it pairs with his other courtroom tag «Заседание продолжается»). The line became a proverb: Russian media still headline stalled projects that finally move with «Лёд тронулся». English coverage is split: the 1961 Richardson translation has 'Things are moving, gentlemen of the jury', Fisher's 2011 Northwestern translation is reported as 'The ice has started breaking up, gentlemen of the jury!', while Wikipedia and Russia Beyond use 'The ice has broken, (ladies and) gentlemen of the jury!'. Published Chinese (张佩文 2004; 白桦熊 2022, whose paratext popularises the sister tag 庭审继续进行) and Japanese (江川卓 1966/1969) renderings of this line could not be retrieved online. The prompt's reference to Durov/VKontakte coverage is unrelated to this term and was not pursued.

rendering.zh: 坚冰已破，陪审员先生们！
rendering.ja: 氷が動き出しましたぞ、陪審員諸君！

value.note_for_reader: Ostap's catchphrase: 'the ice has broken' is the spring river thaw, i.e. things are finally moving; 'gentlemen of the jury' apes a barrister in the Tsarist jury court, abolished in 1917, a mock-solemn anachronism he repeats throughout.

value.finding: An извозчик was a licensed driver of a horse-drawn cab for hire, the ordinary urban taxi of Russian cities before motor transport; the trade split into ломовые (freight carters) and легковые (passenger cabs), and the passenger cabs into cheap peasant 'ваньки', stand-licensed 'биржевые' and expensive 'лихачи'. In 1927 Moscow they were still the everyday way to get across town at night (about 4,900 licensed in 1928, down from ~15,000 before 1917), while motor taxis had only been reintroduced by the Mossovet in December 1924 precisely because cabs, trams and buses were short; by 1934 only 385 remained and the trade was gone by the late 1930s. For a 1928 reader the word carried no exoticism: it was as neutral and daily as 'taxi', with a stock image of a sleepy, grumbling driver on his box, haggling over fares, tipped with a shout of 'Извозчик!' from the pavement. Richardson's 1961 English translation (the text on lib.ru) renders it variously 'cab', 'cabby', 'cab-driver' and, where the horse matters, 'horse-cab' ('His wife took him home in a horse-cab', 'HORSE-CAB NO. 8974'). Japanese has an established equivalent, 辻馬車, used for exactly this Moscow institution by Miyamoto Yuriko in her 1920s essay モスクワの辻馬車, which also transcribes イズヴォシチク and calls the driver 御者. I could not verify online how the Chinese editions (张佩文 2004, 白桦熊 2022) render the word; 马车夫 is the standard dictionary equivalent for a hired-carriage driver in Chinese renderings of Russian literature (e.g. Chekhov's cabman), but I did not confirm it against the Ilf–Petrov text.

rendering.ja: 辻馬車の御者

value.note_for_reader: In 1927 the izvozchik, a horse-drawn cab for hire, was still Moscow's ordinary taxi; motor cabs had only returned in 1924.
value.rationale: All three keep the denotation (a hired horse-drawn cab and its driver, not a taxi) and the plain everyday register, using established forms (Richardson's 'horse-cab', Miyamoto's 辻馬車, dictionary 马车夫); what is given up is the word's total unmarkedness, since 'horse-cab' and 辻馬車 sound faintly period to a modern reader where извозчик did not in 1928. In dialogue the vocative 'Извозчик!' should still go as the short 'Cabby!' / 车夫！ / 御者さん！, with the full rendering kept for narration.

value.finding: Гусище is a fictional district on the edge of Stargorod, introduced in ch. XI: 'Коробейников жил на Гусище — окраине Старгорода. Там жили преимущественно железнодорожники', with a steam engine puffing past behind the houses on an embankment; the archivist Korobeinikov is known there as Варфоломеич. In ch. XIII it is where the new tram depot stands (railway-depot men and rope-makers dug pits there on a 1920 subbotnik), where 'весь Старгород' gathers for the tram opening, and the crowd files 'по Гусищу' under the railway bridge back up into town; the last mention is from the departing train ('Вагоны неслись над Гусищем'), where Ostap spots Alkhen below the embankment. So for a 1928 reader it read as a working-class railwaymen's settlement below the town proper. The name is built like a rustic toponym (гусь 'goose' + place/augmentative suffix -ище, cf. Городище), faintly comic and homely; no real prototype is documented (the Russian Wikipedia article on Starobelsk as the model for Stargorod maps Чмаровка and other features but not Гусище). Existing renderings: Richardson's 1961 English text (lib.ru) has 'Gusishe'; I could not verify Fisher's 2011 spelling, nor the Chinese (张佩文) or Japanese (江川卓) editions online.

value.finding: In the novel an ордер is the slip issued by the Stargorod housing department (жилотдел) when furniture requisitioned from a private house in 1918-19 was handed to an institution or an individual: chapters XI-XII speak of 'копии ордеров, по которым распределялась изъятая из воробьяниновского особняка мебель', of 'пачки ордеров' on Korobeinikov's shelves, of 'зеленые корешки ордеров' (green counterfoils bearing the recipient's address and signature), and of one 'ордер... на десять стульев, выданный музею мебельного мастерства' and another 'на один стул — т. Грицацуеву'. Ushakov's contemporary dictionary gives the sense exactly: 'письменное предписание, распоряжение' with the examples 'ордер на въезд в новый дом' and 'ордер на обувь' — a state chit entitling the holder to receive a specific scarce thing, the everyday paperwork of requisition and rationing; for a 1928 reader it carried the bureaucratic flavour of the housing 'передел' and уплотнение, not a court order or a purchase order. Both established English translations, Richardson (1961) and Fisher (2011), render it simply as 'orders' ('the orders for the distribution of the furniture requisitioned...', 'bundles of orders... green counterfoils'; Fisher pp. 127-139 'the orders according to which the furniture from V...'). I could not reach the text of the Chinese (白桦熊, 上海译文 2022; earlier 张佩文) or Japanese (江川卓, 集英社 1966/1969) translations online, so their renderings are unverified. The prompt's reference to 'Durov and VKontakte, around 2013' does not apply to this 1928 term and was ignored.

value.finding: Уисполком = уездный исполнительный комитет, the executive committee of the uezd (district) soviet: in 1918-1925 the highest organ of power on the territory of a uezd between congresses of soviets, with its own departments (land, military, finance, police, etc.); the uezd tier was abolished in the 1925-29 regionalisation, so by 1928 the word already sounded provincial and slightly dated. 'Гос. № 1' is a state registration plate of the pre-1931 era, when plates were issued locally and the numbering started at 1; the car of the town's top authority naturally holds plate No. 1. In the novel (Part 1, ch. I and III) it is the single official car of the uezd town N, with 'a tiny radiator and a cumbersome body', which has been stuck for two weeks at the corner of Staropan Square and nearly runs Father Fyodor down; the joke is the pomp of the plate against the wreck that carries it. value.finding: Гусище is a fictional district on the edge of Stargorod, introduced in ch. XI: 'Коробейников жил на Гусище — окраине Старгорода. Там жили преимущественно железнодорожники', with a steam engine puffing past behind the houses on an embankment; the archivist Korobeinikov is known there as Варфоломеич. In ch. XIII it is where the new tram depot stands (railway-depot men and rope-makers dug pits there on a 1920 subbotnik), where 'весь Старгород' gathers for the tram opening, and the crowd files 'по Гусищу' under the railway bridge back up into town; the last mention is from the departing train ('Вагоны неслись над Гусищем'), where Ostap spots Alkhen below the embankment. So for a 1928 reader it read as a working-class railwaymen's settlement below the town proper. The name is built like a rustic toponym (гусь 'goose' + place/augmentative suffix -ище, cf. Городище), faintly comic and homely; no real prototype is documented (the Russian Wikipedia article on Starobelsk as the model for Stargorod maps Чмаровка and other features but not Гусище). Existing renderings: Richardson's 1961 English text (lib.ru) has 'Gusishe'; I could not verify Fisher's 2011 spelling, nor the Chinese (张佩文) or Japanese (江川卓) editions online.

value.finding: In the novel this is the state old-women's home in Stargorod, housed in Vorobyaninov's former mansion (the sign Ostap reads in ch. V says «2-й ДОМ СОЦИАЛЬНОГО ОБЕСПЕЧЕНИЯ СТАРГУБСТРАХА»; ch. VIII opens «Завхоз 2-го дома Старсобеса был застенчивый ворюга»), run by the bashful thief Alkhen and filled with his relatives. For a Russian reader the term connotes a Soviet institutional mouthful of an acronym stuck on an old poorhouse, and after the 1971 and 1976 films 'дом Старсобеса' is shorthand for a shabby, pilfered-from welfare home. Both published English translations already use 'Social Security': Richardson (1961) 'the Second Home of Stargorod Social Security (Administration)', elsewhere 'pensioners' home' / 'old-age pensioners' home'; Fisher (2011) 'the Second Stargorod Social Security Home'. No Chinese (Zhang Peiwen 2004, Bai Huaxiong 2022) or Japanese (Egawa Takashi 1966/1977) rendering of this line could be located online.

value.finding: In the novel an ордер is the slip issued by the Stargorod housing department (жилотдел) when furniture requisitioned from a private house in 1918-19 was handed to an institution or an individual: chapters XI-XII speak of 'копии ордеров, по которым распределялась изъятая из воробьяниновского особняка мебель', of 'пачки ордеров' on Korobeinikov's shelves, of 'зеленые корешки ордеров' (green counterfoils bearing the recipient's address and signature), and of one 'ордер... на десять стульев, выданный музею мебельного мастерства' and another 'на один стул — т. Грицацуеву'. Ushakov's contemporary dictionary gives the sense exactly: 'письменное предписание, распоряжение' with the examples 'ордер на въезд в новый дом' and 'ордер на обувь' — a state chit entitling the holder to receive a specific scarce thing, the everyday paperwork of requisition and rationing; for a 1928 reader it carried the bureaucratic flavour of the housing 'передел' and уплотнение, not a court order or a purchase order. Both established English translations, Richardson (1961) and Fisher (2011), render it simply as 'orders' ('the orders for the distribution of the furniture requisitioned...', 'bundles of orders... green counterfoils'; Fisher pp. 127-139 'the orders according to which the furniture from V...'). I could not reach the text of the Chinese (白桦熊, 上海译文 2022; earlier 张佩文) or Japanese (江川卓, 集英社 1966/1969) translations online, so their renderings are unverified. The prompt's reference to 'Durov and VKontakte, around 2013' does not apply to this 1928 term and was ignored.

value.finding: Туальденор is a Russian trade name from French 'toile du nord' ('cloth of the north'): a plain-weave cotton in which white and black threads are woven together to give a grey colour; denser and stronger than calico, and used for cheap men's shirts, smocks, dressing gowns and work clothes (Andreeva, Fashion Encyclopedia 1997; Orlenko 1996; marked as an obsolete term). In chapter VIII ('Голубой воришка') Ilf and Petrov use it five times for the Stargorod old-women's home — the banner 'A brass band is the path to collective creativity', the old women's dresses 'of the very cheapest mouse-coloured tualdenor', the conductor's grey smock and trousers, the cook's cap and apron, and the fire-extinguisher passage — so that the one drab fabric becomes a running joke about institutional poverty. It is a colourless, matter-of-fact fabric name, not slang, and its comic charge comes from repetition plus the pedantic 'мышиного цвета'. Search did not turn up the wording of the Richardson (1961), Fisher (2011), Chinese, or Japanese editions, so no established target rendering could be verified.

rendering.ja: 鼠色の安手の綿布

value.rationale: All three keep the denotation (cheap coarse grey cotton) and the colour word so the repetition and 'туальденоровый чертог' ('a palace of mouse-grey cotton') still land; they give up the loanword's period flavour and its slight obscurity, which no target reader would catch anyway. 'Calico' was avoided in English because it means printed cotton to American readers.

value.finding: «Достойно есть» (Church Slavonic Dostoino yest', Greek Axion Estin) is the Orthodox hymn to the Mother of God sung at the Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom after the anaphora and at the close of most services; its title is simply its first words, 'It is truly meet [to bless thee, O Theotokos]'. In the novel (ch. 3) Father Fyodor, back from Claudia Ivanovna's deathbed with the secret of the chairs, locks himself in the bedroom and hums it 'in a hollow voice' — for a 1928 reader the joke is a priest reflexively chanting the most everyday liturgical hymn while plotting a treasure hunt. Established renderings: English 'It Is Truly Meet' (Wikipedia, OCA; John Richardson's 1961 translation of the novel has 'the prayer It Is Meet'); Japanese Orthodox Church title 「常に福にして」 (Japanese Wikipedia notes the literal 「眞に當れり」 but the church names the hymn by its Japanese incipit); Chinese Orthodox (orthodox.cn prayer books) opens 「称你为有福，确实是理所当然的；永远蒙福，至洁无玷的诞神女…」 and, like Japanese, has no separate short title — the proposed 《理当称颂》 and 「実に当然なり」 are not attested anywhere.

rendering.ja: 「常に福にして」

Given up: the Slavonic archaic flavour of 'есть' and, in zh/ja, the recognisability a 1928 Russian reader had — hence the one-line note.

value.finding: Title of Part I, Chapter XIV (chapter 16 in some editions), where Ostap Bender improvises a secret monarchist 'union' among Stargorod's ex-notables so as to collect 'donations' from them, presenting Vorobyaninov as 'a giant of thought, father of Russian democracy'. The name is a parody of Isaiah 2:4 as it stands in the Church Slavonic/Synodal Bible, 'перекуют мечи свои на орала' (they shall beat their swords into ploughshares): 'орало' is the archaic Slavonic word for a plough, so the name sounds mock-solemn and liturgical while being nonsense, since a pre-revolutionary-style 'Union' named after a peace slogan is absurd (the Soviet state later adopted the very slogan itself, e.g. Vuchetich's 1957 UN statue 'Перекуём мечи на орала'). Wing-word dictionaries record that by the late Soviet and post-Soviet period 'Союз меча и орала' had become a proverbial byword for a sham, paper-only political organisation or conspiracy that exists only in its founders' imagination, and it is still used that way in Russian journalism. Existing translations: Richardson (1961) 'The Alliance of the Sword and Ploughshare'; Fisher (Northwestern, 2011) 'Sword and Plowshare'; Chinese 张佩文 (人民文学, 2004) '剑犁同盟', 徐昌翰 (江苏凤凰文艺, 2022) '剑与犁联合会'; the Japanese 江川卓 translation (1966/1969) is not online and no established Japanese rendering could be found.

value.finding: A fictional square in Stargorod, the invented provincial town of Part One. In the 1928 ZiF text it appears in chapter I ('Безенчук и «нимфы»'): the townspeople gossip about Klavdia Ivanovna's illness 'посреди Старопанской площади, у бюстика поэта Жуковского' with the inscription «Поэзия есть бог в святых мечтах земли», and the executive-committee car 'пересек Старопанскую площадь' through the mud; it recurs as the town's main square (the fire brigade drives out of it). The name is a plausible pre-revolutionary toponym modelled on Moscow's Старопанский переулок in Kitay-gorod, named in 1922 after the locality 'Старые Паны', site of the Polish (панский) trading court documented from 1508; for a Russian reader it simply sounds like an unrenamed old-regime street name, a quiet joke about a town the revolution has not quite reached (an amateur local-history blog identifies it with Kiev's Tsarskaya Square, which is speculation). Both published English translations render it as 'Staropan Square' (John Richardson 1961, verified in the Litres bilingual reader; Anne O. Fisher 2011, per a search snippet of her text). No Chinese (白桦熊 et al.) or Japanese (江川卓, 1969) rendering of this specific square could be verified online.

rendering.ja: スタロパンスカヤ広場

value.rationale: Denotation (a proper name, fixed book-wide) is kept in all three; the connotation of an old Polish-merchant-quarter name left unrenamed is given up, since 'Old Pans' Square' would read as a translated pun the original does not make. English follows the established Richardson/Fisher root-only form; Chinese follows the same root-only convention used for Russian adjectival street names (cf. 特维尔大街, 阿尔巴特广场); Japanese keeps the full feminine form, which is the normal Japanese practice (cf. トヴェルスカヤ通り) and matches the sound the reader sees in the Russian line.

value.finding: ЗАГС = (отдел) записи актов гражданского состояния, the civil-registry office created by the Sovnarkom decree of 18 Dec 1917 that took births, marriages and deaths away from the church's metrical books and made them a purely secular, local-soviet paperwork function; by the 1920s a provincial ZAGS was a small office of a head, a few делопроизводители (paper clerks), an archivist and a typist. Делопроизводитель is the lowest desk grade in Soviet office hierarchy: the person who fills in and files the forms. In the novel Ippolit Matveyevich 'служил в загсе, где ведал столом регистрации смертей и браков' (ch. I), and the phrase itself recurs as a narratorial jab — 'В Ипполите Матвеевиче продолжал бушевать делопроизводитель загса' (ch. value.finding: A fictional square in Stargorod, the invented provincial town of Part One. In the 1928 ZiF text it appears in chapter I ('Безенчук и «нимфы»'): the townspeople gossip about Klavdia Ivanovna's illness 'посреди Старопанской площади, у бюстика поэта Жуковского' with the inscription «Поэзия есть бог в святых мечтах земли», and the executive-committee car 'пересек Старопанскую площадь' through the mud; it recurs as the town's main square (the fire brigade drives out of it). The name is a plausible pre-revolutionary toponym modelled on Moscow's Старопанский переулок in Kitay-gorod, named in 1922 after the locality 'Старые Паны', site of the Polish (панский) trading court documented from 1508; for a Russian reader it simply sounds like an unrenamed old-regime street name, a quiet joke about a town the revolution has not quite reached (an amateur local-history blog identifies it with Kiev's Tsarskaya Square, which is speculation). Both published English translations render it as 'Staropan Square' (John Richardson 1961, verified in the Litres bilingual reader; Anne O. Fisher 2011, per a search snippet of her text). No Chinese (白桦熊 et al.) or Japanese (江川卓, 1969) rendering of this specific square could be verified online.

value.finding: In the novel the word first appears in ch. VI when Ostap fixes his cut: «я, как непосредственный участник концессии и технический руководитель дела, получаю шестьдесят процентов»; from ch. VII on the narrator deadpans «концессионеры знали всё» and uses it as the pair's standing name (ru.wikisource ch. VI, VII). The joke is that a con man and an ex-marshal of nobility hunting chairs style themselves after the NEP-era foreign concessions: under Lenin's decree of 23 Nov 1920 and the Главконцесском (1923) the Soviet state leased mines, oilfields and factories to foreign capital (Harriman manganese, Lena Goldfields, Krupp, the Japanese Sakhalin oil concession); they peaked at 103 in 1926 and were being wound down as the book appeared, so for a 1928 reader концессия was fresh newspaper vocabulary meaning a state-sanctioned, slightly suspect deal in which a foreigner extracts profit from Soviet property. Both English translations (Richardson 1961, Fisher 2011) keep 'concessionaires' / 'the concession' as the running gag. The 张佩文 Chinese version flattens it to 合伙人 and 合同项目, losing the NEP reference, while Chinese historiography of NEP consistently uses 租让 / 租让制 for these concessions; Japanese coverage of the Soviet concessions of the same years (北樺太石油, 1925 treaty) uses 利権 / 利権契約 / コンセッション. The prompt's reference to Durov and VKontakte around 2013 does not apply to this 1928 term and was disregarded.

value.note_for_reader: Концессия: a NEP-era lease of state property to a (usually foreign) private operator; Ostap borrows the term to dignify a two-man treasure hunt.
value.rationale: All three keep the denotation (a state-granted concession, not a mere partnership) and the mock-official register so the running gag survives; en is the established rendering, zh replaces the proposed 特许经营 (modern franchise/PPP jargon) with the term Chinese NEP historiography actually uses, ja keeps 利権 as the word Japanese sources use for the Soviet concessions of the 1920s. What is given up is the reader's instant sense that this was 1926 headline vocabulary, hence the one-line note at first occurrence.

value.finding: Ostap Bender's recurring catchphrase, first spoken in ch. 6 when he takes charge of the chair hunt ("Спокойно, спокойно. За дело берусь я. Заседание продолжается.") and repeated to his final words in the last chapter, where it is paired with "Лёд тронулся, господа присяжные заседатели". It is the formula of a chairman reopening a session after a disturbance, and Dushenko's dictionary of quotations traces it to a famous 'historical utterance': after the anarchist Vaillant's bomb in the French Chambre des députés on 9 Dec 1893, president Charles Dupuy declared "Messieurs, la séance continue!" — a phrase educated Russians of 1928 knew. Bender uses it, together with 'gentlemen of the jury' (jury trials had been abolished in 1917), as a mock-solemn pre-revolutionary judicial/parliamentary register meaning 'the business goes on, nothing has happened'; Friedberg's reader labels its style юридический. The phrase is now proverbial (in Serov's and Dushenko's dictionaries; a 1976 film song title). Established renderings: Richardson (1961, lib.ru text) uses "The hearing is continued" throughout (last words: "The hearing's continued. Things are moving, gentlemen of the jury"), and a TV Tropes summary of the Fisher 2011 translation gives the same "The hearing is continued!"; the 2022 Chinese edition (江苏凤凰文艺, tr. 徐昌翰) makes "庭审继续进行！" the catchphrase and even titles its editor's note with it. No Japanese rendering (江川卓 tr., 1966/1969) could be located online.

rendering.ja: 審理は続行！

value.note_for_reader: Bender's catchphrase: a chairman's formula for reopening a session after a disturbance (Dupuy, Paris 1893: 'la séance continue'), delivered by Bender in the voice of a pre-revolutionary courtroom to his 'gentlemen of the jury'.
value.rationale: All three keep the mock-judicial register that makes the joke and pair naturally with 'gentlemen of the jury' / 陪审员先生们 / 陪審員諸君, and en and zh follow the established published renderings; given up is the literal 'meeting/session' denotation and the Dupuy allusion, which only the note can carry. Bind the fixed wording in every occurrence so it reads as a refrain.
