value.finding: Title of the chapter (XIII in the canonical text, XV in the restored full version) in which Stargorod opens its first tram line on May Day and a newsreel crew films the ceremony. The director 'with the hairy Adam's apple' barks this at the speakers and the crowd — 'Breathe deeper, you are excited!' — ordering the emotion he wants on camera, and the joke is that the excitement is prescribed rather than felt. By 2013 it was a stock Russian catchphrase, quoted deadpan to a person who is agitated or to mock manufactured enthusiasm (it heads blog posts and quote lists on its own). Established renderings: Richardson's English (lib.ru text) titles the chapter 'Breathe Deeper: You're Excited!'; the 2022 Shanghai Translation edition (白樺熊) gives '请深呼吸：您太激动啦！'. No Japanese rendering of the chapter title (江川卓, 1966/1969) was found online, so the ja rendering below is my own.

rendering.ja: 深く息を吸って——あなたは興奮している！

value.rationale: All three keep the denotation and the plural-polite directorial imperative that carries the joke, and en/zh bind to established published renderings; the connotation of a proverb everyone recognises cannot survive translation and is supplied by the note.

value.finding: It is the first line (and title) of Afanasy Fet's 1842 lyric, set to music the same year by A. E. Varlamov as the first-ever Fet romance; by 1850 Apollon Grigoriev called it 'almost a folk song', it appeared in songbooks from the 1850s on and stayed in the repertoire (Lemeshev, Pogudin), so any Russian reader in 1928 or 2013 heard it as a sung tune, not a book poem. In chapter XIV Ostap arrives at 5 a.m. with the widow Gritsatsuyeva's chair and explains, in guillemets, 'Вдовица спит и видит сон. Жаль было будить. «На заре ты ее не буди»' before quoting the note he left signed 'Твой Суслик' — the sentimental parlour romance serves as a mock-tender alibi for sneaking out of the bridal bed with the loot. John Richardson's English (lib.ru) renders it "'Don't wake her at dawn!'", and the romance is catalogued in English as 'Do not wake her at dawn' (ruverses, musopus). A Japanese song-title index glosses it 明け方に　君は彼女を目覚めさせるな and a singing translation by 小野光子 is titled 「あかつきに」; no printed Chinese title for the poem or for this passage of 十二把椅子 was found in search.

value.finding: Fyodor Ivanovich Vostrikov is the priest of the Church of Frol and Lavr in the provincial town N, who hears Madame Petukhova's deathbed confession and becomes the third, solo treasure-hunter; a seminarian who dodged the 1915 draft by taking orders, he is drawn as a petty entrepreneur (rabbits, 'marble' soap, the dreamed-of candle factory), and his letters to his wife parody Dostoevsky; the hunt ends with him mad in the Daryal Gorge. The three address forms are tonally distinct in the text: the narrator calls him 'духовная особа' (chapter XI, 'спросила духовная особа как можно язвительнее'), a mock-solemn officialese label; Vorobyaninov, kicking him over a chair, spits 'святой отец' as pure sarcasm and later sneers 'А святой отец?' inwardly (ch. XII); Bender greets him 'Здравствуйте, батюшка' 'с невыразимой сладостью', the folksy-affectionate form turned into honeyed mockery, before 'многоуважаемый служитель культа' and 'Почем опиум для народа?'. For a Russian reader the name belongs to a national comic canon (Pugovkin in Gaidai's 1971 film; a statue in Kharkov, 2001) and 'опиум для народа' is a proverb. Established renderings: English Richardson (lib.ru) 'Father Theodore Vostrikov', 'Holy Father', 'the cleric'; Fisher (Northwestern, 2011) 'Father Fyodor Vostrikov'; Chinese (Zhang Peiwen, PLPH 2004, Baidu) '神父费多尔' / '费奥多尔神父'; Japanese (Egawa Takashi, Shueisha 1966) 'フョードル神父', with ヴォストリコフ/ボストリコフ both attested.

value.note_for_reader: First line of a Fet poem (1842) sung as a parlour romance every Russian knew; Ostap hums it as his excuse for tiptoeing off with the chair.
value.rationale: All three keep the denotation and the quoted-song-title form (quotation marks / 《》 / 「」) so the reader sees Ostap citing, and the English follows Richardson's established wording; the connotation of a tune everyone can hum is lost in all three and is supplied only by the note, and the archaic 'wake her not' of the earlier proposal was dropped because the romance's own tone is plain and tender, not antique.

value.finding: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov is the co-protagonist of The Twelve Chairs: a 52-year-old (born 1875) former uyezd marshal of the nobility of Stargorod who after 1917 is reduced to a registrar at the ZAGS (civil-registry office) desk for marriages and deaths in the town of N, and who hunts his mother-in-law's jewels with Ostap Bender. His childhood nickname Kisa ('kitty') is what Bender mostly calls him, alongside mock-titles like 'fieldmarshal' and 'district marshal of the Comanches'; the full name-and-patronymic is the narrator's and the pre-revolutionary world's formal address. For Russian readers around 2013 the name is instantly Sergei Filippov's gaunt, pince-nez Kisa from Gaidai's 1971 film (put on a Russian postal envelope in 2012; statues in Pyatigorsk 2008 and Kharkiv) and a byword for a fallen gentleman clinging to dignity, with lines like 'Gentlemen, I have not eaten for six days' in common use. English editions (Richardson 1971, Fisher 2011, Northwestern) and Wikipedia all use 'Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov'. Chinese editions split: Zhang Peiwen (PLPH 2004) and Xu Changhan (Houlang 2022) print 沃洛比亚尼诺夫, and Bai Huaxiong's Shanghai Translation 2022 edition is described with 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇; 沃罗比亚尼诺夫 is the newspaper-table form. Japanese coverage is unsettled (ヴォロビャニノフ in Russia Beyond JP, ヴォロビヤニノフ and ボロビヤニノフ in reviews); Egawa Taku's 1961/1969 translation could not be checked directly.

rendering.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇·沃洛比亚尼诺夫
rendering.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ・ヴォロビャニノフ

value.note_for_reader: Name-and-patronymic (Ippolit Matveyevich) is the polite Russian address; Bender's 'Kisa' (kitty), 'chief' and 'marshal' are his own mocking epithets for the same man.
value.rationale: All three keep the full three-part name so the patronymic's formality and the gap to Bender's nicknames survive; the English form is the established one across both published translations, Chinese follows the two printed editions (沃洛) over the newspaper table (沃罗), Japanese follows the fuller ヴォ/ヴェ spelling used by Russia Beyond JP. Given up: the comic sparrow (воробей) echo in the surname and the reader's film-memory of Filippov, which no transliteration carries.
